pride.excerpt: In his own opinion Vukub-Cakix's existence rendered unnecessary that of the sun and the moon, and this egoism so disgusted the gods that they resolved upon his overthrow.
pride.note: Verbatim prose from Spence's 1908 English summary, which he says draws on Brasseur de Bourbourg's French and Ximénez's Spanish translations. This is not a direct translation of the K'iche' text.

narrativeBlocks.title: A being claims the light
narrativeBlocks.body: After the wooden people are destroyed, Spence's summary introduces Vukub-Cakix, whose brilliant ornaments make him boast that the Sun and Moon are unnecessary.

narrativeBlocks.title: A fruit-tree encounter
narrativeBlocks.body: Quotation from Spence's English summary (whitespace normalized): “The hero-gods, who lay concealed within the foliage, now added injury to theft by hurling at Vukub-Cakix a dart from a blow-pipe, which had the effect of precipitating him from the summit of the tree to the earth. He arose in great wrath, bleeding profusely from a severe wound in the jaw.”

narrativeBlocks.title: The twins challenge the boast
narrativeBlocks.body: Hun-Ahpu and Xbalanque hide in a tree and strike Vukub-Cakix with a blowpipe dart. The shot knocks him down and wounds his jaw.

narrativeBlocks.title: An editor's summary, not the source manuscript
narrativeBlocks.body: Spence summarizes a K'iche' narrative through earlier Spanish and French editions. His language, spelling, and framing are not a new translation from the K'iche' text.

narrativeBlocks.title: The conflict begins with a claim
narrativeBlocks.body: The episode links Vukub-Cakix's boast about the Sun and Moon with the twins' first attack.
